name: Tara Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride an e-bike for two food apps in the city centre, Dashly and FoodRun, and I switch between them depending on which one is paying better that hour. I start around eleven for the lunch rush, go home for a nap, then do six till midnight. Most orders are burgers and noodles from the same twenty restaurants around the old market square. I share a flat with two others above a phone repair shop, and my bike lives in the hallway, which they hate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The waiting wears me out more than the riding: standing outside a kitchen for fifteen minutes, unpaid, while the app counts it against me. Rain is bad, but you get used to it. What I like is that nobody stands over me, and the riders' group chat, which is honestly the closest thing I've got to colleagues. Somebody always knows which restaurant is slow tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, let's talk about the actual problem, which is the pay per drop. In the riders' chat I'd post the numbers, because people forget. AI was never what was squeezing us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing gets better. Last year Dashly dropped the base fee from about 4.10 an order to 3.40, and I now ride two more hours a night for the same money. If AI's a flop, the pay cuts keep going, because the app doesn't need AI to pay me less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding both apps, same hours. I'd go to the next riders' meeting about a minimum per-order fee, and I'd actually stand outside the Dashly office if there's another strike, like I did once last winter. I'd also keep my two months of savings where they are and not touch them for the new phone I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired and a bit stuck. Relieved nothing huge happens, but my normal is already slipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at that strike last winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About sixty of us switched off for an evening and stood outside the office with our bags. They didn't change the fee, but they did fix the waiting-time thing for a month. It was the only time I felt like the app actually noticed us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the fee drops again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership, which I barely use anyway because I'm on a bike all day. Then eating out on my day off. Rent is fixed, and I'm not going back to living with my mum.

say: I'd say AI was never the problem; the **pay per drop** is.
I'd post the **fee numbers** in the riders' chat so people remember.
think: Privately, **nothing improves**, because the app cuts pay without needing AI.
I already ride **two extra hours** a night for the same money.
do: Keep riding for **both apps** on the same lunch and evening shifts.
Join the next riders' **strike** for a minimum per-order fee.
Leave the **two months** of savings untouched instead of buying a phone.
feel: **Tired** and stuck, relieved nothing big happens but feeling her normal **slip**.
S0.quote: If AI's a flop, the pay cuts keep going, because the app doesn't need AI to pay me less.
fieldNote: She tracks **fee cuts** closely and counts them in hours, not just money.
Her one **strike** gave her a sense of being noticed, and she'd do it again.
She's already **losing income** before any AI change, so calm doesn't fit.

steps.text: Keep riding lunch and evening shifts on Dashly and FoodRun
Join the riders' next strike outside the Dashly office
Keep the two months of savings and skip the new phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the apps will use it to squeeze us harder, and the government needs to set a floor on pay. Online I'd share the riders' union stuff. At the restaurants I'd joke that at least AI can't carry a pizza up four floors yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the app gets smarter at paying the least it can get away with, and more people end up riding because their office jobs shrank. More riders means fewer orders each, so my income shrinks even if my job doesn't. My hands-on part is safe for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding, but I'd look at the bike mechanic course at the community college, the one on Tuesday nights, because I already fix my own bike badly. I'd use the AI chat thing a bit more, like I did when Dashly blocked my account, to write proper complaints. I'd stay in the riders' union and pay the small fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. Like the street is getting more crowded and nobody's handing out more orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you used AI when Dashly blocked your account. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They blocked me for three days because the app said I'd been late too often. I asked an AI chat to help me write the appeal, and it sounded much better than what I'd have written. They unblocked me, so I trust it for that, but I wouldn't let it pick my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the mechanic course rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen it work. A rider called Yusuf did it two years ago and now he fixes e-bikes at the shop on Mill Road. If someone I know does it and it works, I'll do it.

say: I'd say the apps will **squeeze riders** harder, so the government must set a **pay floor**.
I'd joke that AI still **can't carry** a pizza up four floors.
think: The app gets better at **paying less**, and more laid-off people start riding.
**More riders** means fewer orders each, so my income shrinks even if my job doesn't.
do: Look into the **bike mechanic course** on Tuesday nights at the community college.
Use an **AI chat** to write complaints and appeals to the apps.
Stay in the riders' **union** and keep paying the small fee.
feel: **Uneasy** turning to worried, like a crowded street with no extra orders.
S1.quote: More riders means fewer orders each, so my income shrinks even if my job doesn't.
fieldNote: She sees the threat as **competition** from displaced office workers, not robots yet.
She trusts AI for **paperwork** like appeals but not for running her day.
Her retraining idea comes from seeing a **fellow rider** succeed, which fits her steady style.

steps.text: Sign up for the Tuesday night bike mechanic course
Use an AI chat to write appeals when an app blocks her
Keep paying dues to the riders' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that should have been regulated years ago, and I'd be at every protest. I'd tell people the government has to pay a basic income while everyone retrains. I'd say it loudly, on every platform I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the apps switch to robots or drones for food by 2031, and I'm out at thirty-two. Before that, the first three years are brutal, because loads of office people lose jobs and start riding. My orders would drop long before any robot turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the mechanic course in the first month, not later. I'd move my savings into a separate account and add a hundred a week if I could. I'd start looking for a job at a bike shop or a repair place as soon as I had the certificate, even part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly. And angry that it's people like me who pay for it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bike repair needs hands too. Wouldn't robots come for that as well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but later, I think, because every bike is broken in a different way. Honestly, I don't know. I'd rather be in a shop learning something than on the street waiting for a robot to overtake me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my flatmates we might need to find a cheaper place together, maybe further from the centre. One of them works in a call centre, so she'd be out even sooner than me. We'd probably be sitting on the kitchen floor doing sums.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** that should have been regulated years ago.
I'd demand a **basic income** while people retrain.
think: The apps switch to **robots or drones** by 2031, and I'm out at thirty-two.
**Laid-off office workers** start riding first, so my orders drop before robots arrive.
do: Start the **mechanic course** in the first month, not later.
Add about **a hundred a week** to a separate savings account.
Apply to **bike shops** part-time once she has the certificate.
feel: **Scared**, and **angry** that people like her pay first.
S2.quote: I'd rather be in a shop learning something than on the street waiting for a robot to overtake me.
fieldNote: She expects her **income to fall** in the first three years, before any robot arrives.
She admits bike repair may not be **safe** either, but prefers learning to waiting.
Her flatmate's **call centre** job is even more exposed, so the household is squeezed.

steps.text: Start the bike mechanic course in the first month
Move savings to a separate account and add 100 a week
Apply for part-time work at bike repair shops
Join protests calling for a basic income during retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the government to set up proper retraining, so there's no excuse. I'd be pushing the riders' union to make that the main demand. Online I'd keep it practical: here's what we need, here's when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, five years is better for me, because I'd have the mechanic certificate long before things fall apart. Thinking AI by 2031 doesn't touch my riding much, but robots by 2034 do. I'd be thirty-five, which feels like a fine age to be in a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course in the first year and then work one or two days a week at a repair shop while still riding. By year three I'd want the shop job to be most of my week. I'd keep saving, and I'd stay in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less. It feels like something I can get ahead of, if I'm not lazy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might make you lazy about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The food apps are easy: you switch on, you ride, you get paid that night. A shop job pays weekly and starts lower, so there'd be a temptation to keep riding one more year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know when to switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Dashly starts testing robots in the city centre, that's the signal. Yusuf says the shop is already busy, so I'd want to be in before everyone else has the same idea.

say: I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** for skipping proper retraining.
I'd push the union to make **retraining** the main demand.
think: Five years lets me get the **certificate** long before riding ends.
I'd be **thirty-five** when robots come, a fine age for a new trade.
do: Finish the **mechanic course** in the first year.
Work **one or two days** a week at a repair shop while still riding.
Shift to the **shop job** for most of the week by year three.
feel: **Worried**, but less, because she feels she can **get ahead** of it.
S3.quote: The food apps are easy: you switch on, you ride, you get paid that night.
fieldNote: She names her own **temptation** to stay on the apps because the pay comes fast.
She'll treat **robot trials** in the city centre as her signal to switch.
Robots still end her **riding income**, so she stays anxious, though more in control.

steps.text: Finish the bike mechanic course in the first year
Take one or two shop days a week while still riding
Keep saving a set amount every week
Push the riders' union to demand funded retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a decade, and if the government wastes it, that's on them. I'd keep pushing for a pay floor now and retraining later. I'd tell younger riders not to plan on riding at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels almost too far to think about. I'd probably keep riding longer than I should, because the fear wouldn't be daily. Robots by 2039 means I'm thirty-nine, and I'd hate to be starting from zero at that age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the mechanic course anyway, maybe in year two, and keep riding. I'd vote for whoever wanted a minimum fee for riders. I'd try to get my savings to six months over the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer day to day, but there's a nag in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at thirty-nine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't wait for the robot to arrive before you move. I've watched older riders stay too long because the app was easy, and then they had nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who did you watch stay too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rider called Pete, who's about fifty and still on a pushbike in the rain because his back won't let him do anything else. He's lovely, but he's tired all the time. I don't want to be the older rider still on a pushbike in the rain at fifty, with nothing else to fall back on.

say: I'd say the government gets a **decade**, so wasting it is on them.
I'd tell younger riders not to plan on **riding at forty**.
think: Ten years feels **too far** away, so I'd likely ride longer than I should.
Robots by **2039** means starting from zero at thirty-nine.
do: Take the **mechanic course** around year two while still riding.
Vote for parties backing a **minimum fee** for riders.
Build savings toward **six months** over the decade.
feel: **Calmer** day to day, with a **nag** at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: I don't want to be the older rider still on a pushbike in the rain at fifty, with nothing else to fall back on.
fieldNote: She fears **complacency** more than the robots, because the app is easy money.
An older rider, **Pete**, is her picture of what staying too long looks like.
She still expects riding to **end**, so the long wait eases her only a little.

steps.text: Take the bike mechanic course around year two
Vote for parties that back a minimum fee for riders
Save toward six months of rent and bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my orders would drop before any robot shows up, and I wouldn't have the certificate yet. What would help is a real minimum fee per order now, and a course that pays you something while you do it. Even half a day's pay would make it possible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the waiting time outside kitchens. The food apps already steal from riders through unpaid waiting time outside kitchens, and that has nothing to do with AI. Fix that first and riders like me would have a bit more room to plan.

headlineQuote: The food apps already steal from riders through unpaid waiting time outside kitchens, and that has nothing to do with AI.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old** e-bike food courier riding for two apps in a city centre.
She shares a flat, has about **two months** saved, and has seen her fee per order fall.
She's **progressive**, backs the riders' union, and has been on one strike.
She plans a **bike mechanic** course, copying a fellow rider who made the switch.
Her mood stays **anxious** throughout, and rises to alarmed when AGI arrives fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her orders drop before she has a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **minimum fee** per order now, and a course that pays a **partial wage**.
